name: B. C. Mohanty
title: B. C. Mohanty: Reading the Work Inside a Textile
description: Through studies of ikat, natural dyes and other crafts, Bijoy Chandra Mohanty helped preserve knowledge of how textiles are made and the working lives behind them.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs.text: English words run across a silk souvenir made in the Nuapatna area for the coronation of George VI in 1937. In the 1974 book Ikat Fabrics of Orissa and Andhra Pradesh, it appears as Calico Museum object 2280. Its photograph and caption bring together a textile, a place and an occasion.

Bijoy Chandra Mohanty, usually credited as B. C. Mohanty, wrote that book with Kalyan Krishna. Published by the Calico Museum of Textiles in Ahmedabad, it assigns the historical study to both authors and the technical and socioeconomic study to Mohanty. Dr Moti Chandra edited the volume.

The souvenir is a useful way into his work. A pattern can carry words; a piece of cloth can remember an event. Understanding it calls for attention to the object’s construction as well as its history. Mohanty’s part in the study brought those questions into contact with the working lives of weavers.

The museum’s description of the later revised ikat volume shows the range of the undertaking: historical background, comparison of techniques, fabric analysis and the conditions of weavers. It lists sketches, photographs and actual cloth samples alongside the text. The samples were included as material for further study and research.

This gives a reader several ways into a textile. A photograph preserves an appearance; a drawing can clarify a process; a sample allows the material itself to remain part of the enquiry. A book assembled in this way asks to be studied closely, with comparisons between what is described and what can be seen.

sections.title: The working life behind the pattern

paragraphs.text: In its account of Odisha in 1974, the ikat study discusses family participation, seasonal farming work, cooperative societies, master weavers and the supply of yarn. These passages describe the circumstances recorded then. They bring production and livelihood into the same enquiry as technique.

These concerns change the questions a reader brings to a sari. Who supplied the yarn? Who prepared it? How did cloth leave the loom and reach a buyer? Recording those relationships gives the maker a place in textile history beyond the praise attached to a finished design.

Mohanty’s published work also reaches beyond ikat. Natural Dyeing Processes of India appeared through the Calico Museum in 1987, jointly authored with K. V. Chandramouli and H. D. Naik. Its subject places colour-making alongside the study of weaving. The author credit also reminds us that this body of documentation was built through collaboration.

Other catalogue records identify his Applique Craft of Orissa and Patachitras of Orissa, both published in 1980 with Alfred Bühler as general editor. For Block Printing and Dyeing of Bagru, Rajasthan, published in 1983, he worked with Jagadish Prasad Mohanty. These titles place his contribution across several kinds of making and more than one region.

For a reader in Odisha, this work offers a way to follow familiar crafts beyond their broad names. Looking closely means recognising different materials and operations, and making room for the people whose work gives them form. It also means keeping the distinction between the craftsperson’s knowledge and the scholar’s record of it.

The Nuapatna souvenir holds a public occasion in the threads of a small piece of silk. Mohanty’s work helps keep such details available for another reader: the place, the object and the skill that made it possible.

original_scan.coverage: Selected pages only, not a complete reading. PDF has no extracted text. Title/credit leaves, preface, contents, two plate-list pages, complete socioeconomic section, summary opening and one plate page inspected.

corrections: Expand initials to Bijoy Chandra from original title leaf; do not infer identity from surname alone.
Credit Kalyan Krishna for the 1974 joint book and historical research; technical/socioeconomic research specifically credits B. C. Mohanty.
Credit K. V. Chandramouli and H. D. Naik for Natural Dyeing Processes of India.
Keep the later 2003/2004 edition discrepancy visible in the source note; do not transfer its sample/page counts to 1974.
Do not invent museum employment title, birth/death dates, education, awards or training lineage.
Do not turn documentation into a claim that he invented, single-handedly saved or revived the crafts.
inspection_limits: Calico revised-edition description read; revised physical book not inspected.
CiNii pages available as indexed primary catalogue text; direct opens returned cache misses.
Natural-dye and other monographs not read; no recipe, chemical or fieldwork claims derived from their titles.
